Chapter 3: Letting Go of Fear and Limiting Beliefs
Have you ever noticed how fear can quietly sneak into your life? Sometimes it’s loud—like that rush of nerves right before a big decision. Other times, it’s quieter. Maybe just a hint of self-doubt, or that little hesitation that holds you back.
Let’s take a closer look at how these fears, and the beliefs we hold about ourselves, can shape our choices—sometimes without us even realizing it. When we let go of these patterns, we open the door to more freedom and greater possibilities.
Picture this: you’re standing at the edge of something new. Maybe it’s a job offer, a move to a new city, or finally chasing a dream you’ve held close for years. You feel excited, but there’s also anxiety bubbling up. What if it doesn’t work out? What if you fail? Your mind starts spinning stories of everything that could go wrong, and suddenly, the urge to play it safe gets stronger. Sound familiar?
Here’s something to remember: fear isn’t the enemy. It’s actually a messenger. It points to places where you can grow, where old stories are ready to be rewritten. So many of our beliefs come from childhood, from our culture, or from things we’ve been through in the past. These beliefs—about what’s possible, what’s safe, or what we’re allowed to do—often run in the background, quietly steering us without us even noticing.
Maybe you remember being told as a kid to “be careful,” or to avoid taking risks. Over time, those messages become part of your inner world, forming a kind of protective shell. But as life goes on, you might start to feel that shell closing in, keeping you from adventure, meaning, or deeper connections.
So, what can you do? The book offers some gentle practices. When fear pops up, instead of fighting it or letting it take over, try pausing for a moment. Listen to what the fear is saying. What’s it trying to protect? Is there real danger—or just an old story playing out in your mind? By getting curious about your fear, you’ll find its grip starts to loosen.
Think about someone who’s been afraid of public speaking for years. The first time they step up to the mic, their hands shake, their voice wobbles. But instead of beating themselves up, they approach it with kindness and curiosity. Each time they try, the fear shrinks just a little, and confidence starts to grow. It becomes clear: courage isn’t the absence of fear. It’s moving forward, even when you’re scared.
Letting go of limiting beliefs isn’t a one-and-done thing. It’s a practice. Start by noticing the stories you tell yourself—about what’s possible, about your worth, or about the world. Most of these stories aren’t ones you chose; they were handed down to you. By bringing them into the open, you give yourself the chance to choose differently.
The Field—that sense of openness and possibility—responds when you let go of fear and judgment. Suddenly, you’re more open to inspiration, to new connections, and to joy. Life stops feeling like a test, and starts feeling like an adventure.
So as you move forward, try this: notice where fear shows up. Meet it with curiosity. And remember—every belief is just a story, and every story can be rewritten.
